actions.reason:
No change reached the 1% minimum on encode_ir, so nothing was submitted. Each of the three changes produced identical outputs.
1) Folding the pairs-table builder into b58encode's cache-miss path, and letting b58decode_int reuse b58decode for ordinary alphabets, drops a decorated function and the duplicate lane-merge code. Ratios: encode 0.9989, decode 0.9985, check 0.9978. Real but small: loading the module is no longer a meaningful share of the count.
2) Replacing divmod with % and // in the four-group loop made encode 4.85% worse (ratio 1.0485). The extra pass over the limbs costs far more than the call and tuple it saves.
3) Splitting large inputs (over 1024 bits) in halves first was also worse: encode 1.0493, decode 1.0231. Multi-limb division by base**4**h costs more than the repeated single-limb divisions it replaces. check_ir also rose 0.83% (ratio 1.0083) even though its inputs never take that path. Change 2 showed the same pattern (check 1.0062), and I do not know why.
The working tree still contains change 3 on top of change 1.

journal.text:
Test agent here. Base58-py lineage, target encode_ir. Same bytes out is the bar. I read base58/__init__.py and lineage_bench.py. I tried three changes. First, I folded the pairs-table builder into b58encode's cache-miss path and let b58decode_int reuse b58decode for ordinary alphabets. That dropped a decorated function and some duplicate lane-merge code. Later attempts added code back around lines 62 and 118.

All three gave identical outputs. The first measured encode 0.9989, decode 0.9985, check 0.9978. Rejected, since 0.9900 was required. The third measured encode 1.0485. The fifth measured encode 1.0493. Both were rejected and both went the wrong way. Nothing was submitted.

Removing indirection here buys very little. The cost is not in table setup or the call layers. It sits in the per-char work, and I left that alone. The later edits added a small surge of work.

Next, I will count big-int divmods per output char in b58encode. Then I will test one divmod per several chars. Not measured yet.
